title: Programmers' revolt against the 996 overtime system has caught the world's attention. How did it organize and spread, in programmers' own way?
excerpt: It began as one person's complaint. Now it is the work of a 160,000-strong community, collaborating the way open-source software gets built.
body:
It began as one person's complaint. Now it is the work of a 160,000-strong community, collaborating the way open-source software gets built.

A protest over labor rights broke out this past week and turned 996 — the 9 a.m. to 9 p.m., six-day-a-week overtime schedule that Chinese internet companies have grown used to — into a focus of attention in China and around the world.

A group of programmers launched [996.ICU](https://996.icu/#/zh_CN), a project against the 996 work schedule. The discussion started in tech communities, spread through the WeChat groups of internet companies, moved on to Douban and Zhihu, and was soon trending on Weibo. Search interest in "996" on Baidu [reached ten times its normal level](http://index.baidu.com/v2/main/index.html#/trend/996?words=996). The project's founder pinned coverage from *China Youth Daily* and *Southern Daily* to the project's information page.

Over the week, the story spread abroad. The first English-language outlet to follow up was the China-focused [South China Morning Post](https://www.scmp.com/tech/start-ups/article/3003691/developers-lives-matter-chinese-software-engineers-use-github), whose March 29 report was retweeted by Python's creator, [Guido van Rossum](https://twitter.com/gvanrossum), with a one-line comment: "996 is inhumane."

On Hacker News and the corresponding Reddit forums, where programmers around the world gather, 996 became a hot topic too. [The Verge](https://www.theverge.com/2019/4/2/18291035/chinese-developers-github-protest-long-work-hours) and the [Financial Times](https://www.ft.com/content/72754638-55d1-11e9-91f9-b6515a54c5b1) followed up on April 2 and April 3, and outlets including *Wired* were already interviewing participants.

Unlike Chinese manufacturing workers, who drew global attention a year or two ago through tragedy, programmers look like the group least likely to fight over their working conditions. The outside impression of them is that they earn well, are used to working late every day, keep camp beds in the office, and live simply while saving to buy an apartment and get married — a classic middle-class profession, and the middle class is usually thought of as both important to any revolution and the greatest source of resistance to one.

But unlike other industries where overtime is just as routine, the hours harder and the pay worse, programmers have a channel to speak through.

### 1

The domain 996.icu was registered by a young programmer.

On the tech forum V2EX, this user once mentioned, in a thread about pay, that he had graduated from a Project 211 university in Beijing, worked at a large internet company on a par with Baidu, Alibaba and Tencent, had just come off probation, and earned a bit over 10,000 yuan a month.

Before that, his posts on the forum were about technical matters — about why pay differed between teams inside the same company. But recently his company had started running on 996.

On March 20, he announced in the forum's domain-promotion section that he had registered the domain http://996.icu, with the slogan: "Work 996, get sick, end up in the ICU."

After March 26 he replied under a thread about workplaces: "Only now do I see how much 996 wrecks you — all I do is work and rest, and I barely talk to my family anymore." In that reply he recommended the 996.ICU site again.

[996.ICU](https://996.icu/#/zh_CN) is just a website, split from top to bottom into three parts: an introduction to 996, seventeen laws and regulations on labor rights, and reports on related events. All three were there from the first day, though the content has grown much richer over the past week.

![The 996.icu website](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20190403234205nrUKDQwbkNl75eWJ.jpg-w600)

The site's author also added the line "Developers' Lives Matter" after the introduction, echoing "Black Lives Matter," the slogan of the American movement against racial inequality.

Its influence did not come from this web page, though. It came from the [GitHub project that went up the same day, March 26](https://github.com/996icu/996.ICU).

The project was started by an anonymous account named 996icu, and its relationship to the domain's owner is unknown. But judging by how quickly it handles as many as 260 suggestions a day, even if the account was created by that young programmer, it is probably no longer he alone who uses it.

![](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20190404000735djQuI3xlZVJnctG7.jpg-w600)

Software development today no longer means reinventing the wheel every time — open-source code lets you finish a feature fast.

GitHub is the largest platform holding that code. Programmers use it to manage their projects, start discussions and submit suggested changes.

GitHub now [has 30 million programmer users](http://www.sohu.com/a/276484595_671058), hosts about 80 million code repositories, and sees 1.6 new repositories created every second on average. In 2018, [Microsoft announced it would buy GitHub for $7.5 billion.](https://techcrunch.com/2012/07/14/what-exactly-is-github-anyway/)

GitHub had already hosted projects about overtime at Chinese internet companies. Two months ago, one titled ["Programmer Job Blacklist"](https://github.com/shengxinjing/programmer-job-blacklist) went up, and within two months it had collected more than 18,000 "stars."

But that one reads more like a practical handbook for programmers looking for work. 996.ICU is more direct and simpler: from the start it was a manifesto against the 996 system.

That let it strike a chord fast.

996 has never had a good name. The earliest reports go back to [a 2014 case in which a pregnant Alibaba employee worked overtime, went home and died of severe hemorrhaging](http://it.sohu.com/20140405/n397797427.shtml). In 2016, [58.com drew a great deal of pushback for forcing 996 on more than 20,000 employees](http://finance.cnr.cn/gs/20160901/t20160901_523105136.shtml).

This January, [the CEO of Hangzhou-based Youzan](http://www.linkshop.com.cn/web/archives/2019/418163.shtml) announced out of nowhere at the company's annual meeting that 996 would be mandatory across the company; a Youzan executive said that if employees could not balance work and family, they could choose to get divorced.

More recently, JD.com began running on a 995 schedule in early March. Facing criticism, [JD.com's PR director, Liu Li, replied that it would not be compulsory, but that employees were encouraged to throw themselves into their work](http://tech.163.com/19/0312/13/EA2QGIOK00097U7R.html).

Overtime at Chinese internet companies has never been treated as an exception, but it used to carry the promise of a big payoff. In 2017 the average salary in the software industry was 133,000 yuan, beating finance for the second year running to become the country's best-paying industry. When Alibaba listed on the New York Stock Exchange, it made more than 10,000 people worth over 10 million yuan overnight.

The wave of listings that began in 2018 produced no second Alibaba. Xiaomi was valued at $45 billion in 2014, and before its 2018 listing the company was expected to be worth $80 billion to $100 billion, which would have doubled the value of the stock held by employees of four years' standing. But by early 2019, when employees could finally sell, Xiaomi's market value had shrunk to $31.5 billion and the stock was worth 30 percent less than in 2014.

And Xiaomi was one of the better performers among the past year's listings. [Mogujie diluted its employees' equity outright, cutting the value of their holdings to one twenty-fifth.](https://www.jiemian.com/article/2703824.html) Mogujie's listing price was $14; 10,000 shares should have been worth 966,000 yuan, but after a 25-fold dilution they came to 40,000 yuan.

Even the job itself was no longer a sure thing. A few years ago the internet industry was riding high and venture money poured in. Startups did not worry about profit and could offer higher salaries to poach people.

Things have changed. In 2018, VC and PE fundraising in China came to $34.112 billion, [a fall of 74.59 percent from the year before](https://36kr.com/p/5150552). Internet companies that had grown by burning cash ran into the profit question once they listed. With the money supply gone, layoffs became a common way to cut losses.

Last August, Meitu and Lagou each cut 20 percent of their staff. In October, Smartisan dissolved its Chengdu branch, and the programmers it had moved there from Beijing lost their jobs too. In November, Qudian cut 200 people — anyone unwilling to move from Beijing to Hangzhou had to go as well — and Douyu cut 70 the same month. In December, Zhihu cut 20 percent, with 300 people told to leave the same day; iFlytek cut 20 percent and called it culling the bottom performers; Mobike cut 30 percent and called it a normal adjustment. This February, Didi cut 15 percent, 2,000 people; JD.com first cut 20 percent of its staff, then in February cut 10 percent of its vice-president-level executives. In March, Tencent cut 20 percent of its middle managers, which [Tencent President Martin Lau called](http://m.kanshangjie.com/Index/Show?id=161549) a deliberate move to bring in younger blood.

Heavy work grew heavier, the listing story people once counted on receded, and against a backdrop of mass layoffs even how many years the job would last became hard to know.

That is the background against which 996.ICU collected more than 2,000 stars within an hour of going up, passed 10,000 stars within a day, and climbed onto GitHub's live trending chart.

More people noticed.

### 2.

Anony began following it within an hour of 996.ICU going live on March 26. He calls himself an ordinary coder who likes browsing GitHub in his spare time; browsing GitHub, he says, is "like you guys scrolling Weibo."

Although Anony's own company does not run on 996, he kept watching the project's progress and helped edit its wording.

In 996.ICU's discussion section — the Issues page — just before the star count passed 100,000, someone wrote that they had never expected to take part in a large open-source project this way.

On social networks people share their own experiences of 996, their views and their proposed solutions. But inside the programmer community, everything moves the way programmers build open-source software.

Imagine a building full of countless meeting rooms, each with a whiteboard carrying all the code for one piece of software. GitHub lets a programmer walk into any of the open rooms, watch the code on the whiteboard ("Watch"), give it a thumbs-up ("Star"), and change it as he sees fit.

But changing it at will would scramble the code on the whiteboard, so GitHub's core feature is the fork: a user copies the whole codebase on the whiteboard into his own account, where his edits do not touch the project's code. When the edits are done, he can send a "pull request" to the project's maintainers to merge his changes into the project.

That is how open-source software is built together online today, and 996.ICU has evolved by exactly this method.

The [first version of 996.ICU on GitHub was simple](https://github.com/996icu/996.ICU/commit/87de776ac2c22174cbb3a554e89a0ff2a1fadcc5#diff-04c6e90faac2675aa89e2176d2eec7d8): a 26-line Markdown web document.

Excerpts from labor law, the origins of May Day, the lyrics to "The Internationale" and an English version were among the first updates.

Every addition and refinement to 996.ICU came through participants filing pull requests, until it became what it is today.

This is not like leaving a comment on a forum: anyone who feels uneasy at the sight of code cannot file a change request here.

Details were fixed quickly. One request pointed out that JD.com, one of the cases on the main page, would mean nothing to foreign investors if transliterated as "JINGDONG," and should be changed to "JD.COM."

Capitalization, spacing, broken links and misused full-width and half-width punctuation were all corrected and folded into the Markdown document, and someone uploaded a logo he had made himself.

Translations into French, German, Italian, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese, Brazilian Portuguese, Thai, Traditional Chinese, Vietnamese, Russian, Greek and other major languages were all submitted on the project's second day online. Someone even wrote a [fairly formal Classical Chinese version](https://github.com/996icu/996.ICU/pull/16430/files%E3%80%81): "The system called '996': each day the laborer takes his post at the ninth hour of the morning and toils on until the ninth hour of the night, six days in every week. Since the ninth month of the year 2016, word hath spread across the web that 58.com imposeth the 996 system upon its whole staff, and pays not a coin for labor on the rest days…"

March 28 was the first day of fast progress: the project acquired two companion projects, a [996 Company Blacklist](https://github.com/fengT-T/996_list) and a [955 Company Whitelist](https://github.com/formulahendry/955.WLB).

The blacklist held companies that run on 996 or on excessive overtime; nearly every big Chinese internet company is on it, with JD.com far ahead at more than 1,200 votes. The author also asked that nominations include the department, the province and the salary range — in short, the more detail the better.

The blacklist's author had originally set the voting up on a forum, and had not expected so many people to take part; the site got so slow that people only noticed the big companies at the top. He is now building a new site, and wrote in the project description: "Because it was so slow, everyone only noticed the big companies up top. I hope people will see that the group hit by 996 is actually huge — it isn't only BAT, there are plenty of small companies too."

The whitelist, by contrast, was mostly foreign companies.

The 955 Company Whitelist's author, formulahendry, is a programmer at a large foreign company in Shanghai. His GitHub page has more than 600 followers, and he kept a technical blog in English for a while.

Like almost all foreign companies, formulahendry's employer does not require 996. He told QDaily that 996 leaves no personal life at all, that it has been getting more common lately, and that this is not a good trend. His objection to 996 is the same as many people's: compared with a 40-hour week, the 72-hour 996 week does not produce more per hour worked.

After noticing 996.ICU, he decided that rather than griping about 996, it would be more useful to look at which companies run on 995 — five days a week, 9 a.m. to 5 p.m.

On the project's second day he created the whitelist vote. He made up the name WLB himself, short for Work Life Balance. WLB passed 1,000 stars within a day and reached GitHub's live trending chart on its second day online.

The first version of the vote rested on formulahendry's own knowledge of Shanghai's IT companies. Over the following days he kept the project up to date using the ride home on the company shuttle and his weekends.

Although formulahendry built the whitelist, once the project existed it was no longer his alone to decide: everything had to go GitHub's way.

The 996 Company Blacklist drew even more participation. Adding a company to it is not very different from reviewing code for an open-source project: anyone can submit evidence, though the way evidence has to be submitted is something of a barrier for non-programmers. The evidence includes media reports, Zhihu discussions and company announcements.

Whether Huawei and [companies such as ByteDance](https://github.com/996icu/996.ICU/pull/24767) belonged on the list set off a great deal of argument. Under a request to "remove ByteDance from the blacklist" there were 51 threads of conversation, with those who wanted it removed and those who did not each presenting evidence.

The user who filed the removal request gave two reasons. First, employees leave late but also arrive late, and counting lunch and the break after dinner, actual working time does not reach 12 hours a day; the company runs on a big-week/small-week schedule, but pays overtime for the Sunday of a small week. Second, the programmer whose sudden death set off the controversy had only recently moved to ByteDance from Tencent, so the death could not simply be pinned on overtime at ByteDance.

One rebuttal ran: "You'd think companies on 955 don't take a lunch break or eat dinner." Others pointed to sleight of hand in how overtime pay is worked out — Sunday overtime paid at 1.2 times the normal wage instead of twice, for instance.

Whether a request passes comes down to a simple vote. The request to remove ByteDance drew 8 in favor and 269 against. In the end, 996.ICU's maintainer rejected it.

The account running the project can rule on requests, but because open-source projects can be freely copied, a founder who strays too far from what most of the community wants will find that programmers can easily shift their support to another project forked from this one.

Once a personal project turns into a community project, its direction is no longer decided by the founder but by everyone who contributes to it. This is simply how open-source software is made.

Linux, for example, started as one man's work: Linus Torvalds'. But as developers around the world joined in, some 15,000 developers and more than 1,400 companies have added bricks to it. Linux today is far beyond Linus's control; a dedicated foundation runs it.

996.ICU is no different. Whoever started the project, it is no longer one person's to decide.

### 3.

The discussion turned sensitive on March 29, when the project's [Issues section was closed](https://github.com/996icu/996.ICU/issues).

The sudden closure of the repository's discussion section set off plenty of talk of its own: too many issues (past 100,000), too many ads, and some people posted screenshots of a call for a White House petition and suspected political reasons. A few hours later the author posted an explanation: closing it had been his own choice.

It made little difference to the discussion. Early on, someone posted QR codes for WeChat groups in various cities, and someone else replied that programmers should use programmers' tools, not QQ and WeChat, to talk to one another. So Slack, the messaging tool programmers use, and Discord, the gaming chat tool, were both put to work, and a 996.ICU discussion group appeared on Telegram, which cannot be reached directly from inside China.

996.ICU's Slack channel drew more than 1,000 members in five days, and members split the group into channels for announcements, hiring, general discussion, Chinese, English, cities and more. The most discussed subject on Slack was what to do once your labor rights have been violated.

[Chen Hao, a programmer with twenty years' experience](https://www.zhihu.com/question/317847010/answer/636013957), answered a question on Zhihu: "Besides launching a protest on GitHub, what other clever ways are there to resist 996?" He proposed legal action, petitioning the government through the xinfang system, and collective protest.

In the Slack discussion his proposals ran into a good deal of resistance. Some members questioned how effective labor arbitration is; others worried that petitioning could bring coercive measures from the authorities.

After the wording, the language versions and the blacklist and whitelist had all been polished, 996.ICU's biggest step since last weekend has been taking the anti-996 software license from an idea to a real document.

On March 27, [an idea was hotly discussed and then adopted](https://github.com/996icu/996.ICU/pull/15642): design a software license built around labor protections, the 996ICU License. If it were folded into the licenses of open-source projects, companies that run on 996 would not be allowed to use those projects — a real constraint on companies.

Labor law has always been there; enforcement is the problem. A big internet company often supplies tens of thousands of jobs to a city, and some deliver billions or even more than ten billion yuan in taxes and profits. In theory a local court — Shenzhen's, say — should treat Tencent, Huawei and their employees fairly. But that is in theory.

A software license, on the other hand, is a constraint from inside the software industry. Put simply, a software license is like the copyright notice in a book. Using open-source software in a project is all but unavoidable; it costs nothing to use, but you have to follow the terms the author sets out in the license. If a company or an individual uses open-source code without following those terms, the author can sue, demanding damages or that they stop using the code.

The idea drew upvotes from more than a thousand people, and over 400 took part in discussing the license.

But no one had worked out how to write it. At first there were only three lines:

- The 996ICU License (996ICU)
- Copyright © 2019 <copyright holders>
- <wait to be filled...>

On the night of March 30, Katt Gu, a doctor of law from the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign, spent the whole night drafting it. The version she produced is adapted from [the widely used MIT open-source license](https://github.com/kattgu7/Anti-996-License/wiki). The license has three clauses; beyond the standard copyright notice every license carries, Katt Gu added two:

> The individual or legal entity must strictly comply with all applicable laws, regulations, rules and standards relating to labor and employment in the jurisdiction where the individual is physically located, or was born or naturalized, or where the legal entity is registered or does business (whichever is stricter). If no such laws, regulations, rules and standards exist in that jurisdiction, or if that jurisdiction's laws, regulations, rules and standards are not enforceable, then the individual or legal entity must comply with the core conventions of international labor standards.
> The individual or legal entity shall not in any way induce or force its full-time or part-time employees, or its independent contractors, to agree orally or in writing to directly or indirectly restrict, weaken or relinquish the rights or remedies they hold under laws, regulations, rules and standards relating to labor and employment, regardless of whether such written or oral agreement is recognized by the laws of that jurisdiction. Nor shall such individual or legal entity restrict in any way its employees' or independent contractors' right to report or complain about the above violations of the license to the copyright holder or to the authorities that oversee compliance with the license.

Katt Gu works on legislation around new technology, and has written papers on [the gap between law and practice in particular fields in China](https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=PTcpQwcAAAAJ&hl=en&oi=ao).

On the night of March 29, Katt Gu's husband, the entrepreneur Suji Yan, who [has long followed how software copyright has evolved](https://www.qdaily.com/articles/23804.html), saw 996.ICU and pressed her to draft a license. Gu recalls that at first she did not want to.

"Because I'm a workaholic myself. But think about it and this is really about voluntary choice," Gu told QDaily. Her hesitation also came from her training: drafting this license meant research across IP law, labor law and international conventions, none of which she had worked on before.

Before she started, a lawyer told her that to do the license justice she would have to study labor law for ten years, then IP law for another ten — or find ten experts in each of the fields involved to discuss and research the question before drafting anything.

But Katt Gu felt the license's practical effect mattered far less than its effect as a statement, and that even today's most important open-source licenses were not produced through that kind of legislative process in the first place.

After a night of research, she decided to build the draft on the simplest possible base, common law, using the simple and widely used MIT open-source license as her template.

The license, and the effect it hopes to have, are both fairly idealistic.

In Suji Yan's ideal case, the license could put a real constraint on Chinese internet companies. His logic: software development today is essentially impossible without open-source code — Microsoft was at one point the largest contributor to open-source software. Once enough open-source projects use the 996ICU license, a company that forces 996 on its employees puts its own product in breach of the license, and the owners of the open-source code can sue it. Even if suing in mainland China is hard, most of these companies are listed in Hong Kong or the United States, so suits could be filed elsewhere.

Having laid all this out, he added: "This is of course an extremely idealistic scenario."

"I used to think that if we didn't do it, someone else would. But now I think it really does need more people paying attention," Katt Gu said. After the license was published she got a thank-you email. "It felt like a doctor receiving one of those silk banners praising his miraculous healing hands."

Doubt about how binding the license really is, is common, and there is no shortage of outright opponents. Evan You, the creator of what is currently GitHub's third-largest project, wrote on Weibo that he personally opposes and condemns 996, but also opposes putting a discriminatory clause — one that bars certain users — into an open-source project's license, or using an open-source project for political maneuvering of any kind.

"I have my own personal views, but the project is neutral. Vue's license will not ban anyone from using it, not now and not later," he wrote on Weibo. Vue.js is a framework for building web user interfaces.

Still, the number of projects adding the anti-996 license [keeps rising](https://github.com/996icu/996.ICU/blob/master/awesomelist/projects.md). So far 75 open-source projects have added it. Most are maintained by individual developers, but several open-source projects with four or five thousand stars and up — sizable ones used by many companies — have joined as well. Several plugin projects related to Vue have also adopted the anti-996 license: once an open-source project grows large enough, it is no longer the author's alone to decide.

Katt Gu says her next task is to revise the license so that it is compatible with more of the mainstream open-source licenses, the only way it stands a chance of being taken up by more projects.

"I just want to write this license well. Once it's written, it probably won't need me anymore. Writing it in detail could take two or three years." Katt Gu said she probably will not stay involved once this is done. Suji Yan added: "Give it back to the community."

The community has a larger goal. On April 1, someone called for adding the anti-996 license to GitHub's official list of licenses, so that new open-source projects could adopt it easily.

The longer-range goal is to get GitHub to highlight it, so that any project choosing a license at setup would have a chance to see it.

None of this is easy. Getting highlighted on the front page in particular requires more than 1,000 public projects using the license, three star projects adopting it, and approval from the OSI and GNU.

Richard Stallman, one of the forces behind open-source software, published the *GNU Manifesto* in 1985, arguing that all software should carry the spirit of free software — the freedom to run, copy, distribute, study, modify and improve it.

But from the beginning this movement never stopped at technology or at getting software for nothing: its founders held that any application the public can reach should be entirely in the hands of its users. If the 996.ICU contributors' plan works, it will be the first recognized license in open-source software to set out labor rights.

In less than a week, the counterattack on 996.ICU had already arrived.

No company would dare attack GitHub directly. A sustained attack in 2015 [did not work](https://www.qdaily.com/articles/7938.html). Now that it belongs to Microsoft, a commercial company attacking it would be even less sensible.

So the attackers used the method they know best: blocking.

From March 30, people in the Slack group started reporting errors: inside WeChat, in the Beijing area, 996.ICU's GitHub page would not open. Further testing showed this was not an isolated case.

QQ Browser said the site contained fraudulent information. WeChat's stated reason was: "This page contains illegal or non-compliant content. Access has been stopped in order to maintain a clean online environment." Alibaba's UC Browser and 360 Browser both classified the page as a site containing illegal information. Strangest of all, Cheetah Browser threw up a warning on opening the page: "This site contains a large amount of obscene and pornographic material."

Search "996" on Baidu and the Chinese-language results contain no link to the 996.icu site or its GitHub page.

What is different this time is that none of this can wipe out 996.ICU's existence, or make the channels where people discuss it disappear.
